results.answer: Yes, you can do a quick sum without opening the full calculator using the Quick Calculator mode. This will sum the column and return a vector of the result [4] and [5] — the Quick Calculator handles this without opening a full window. The exact command for summing a column is `C-x * :`, which is part of the Quick Calculator mode [2] and [4]

results.answer: Yes, you can have a template inserted automatically whenever you create a new file of a given type using the `auto-insert-alist` and `auto-insert` variables in Emacs. Specifically, you define entries in `auto-insert-alist` where the CAR is a mode name or a regexp matching the file name, and the CDR specifies what to insert (a file or skeleton) or a function to call. When a new file is created, Emacs checks `auto-insert-alist` and, if a match is found, inserts the specified template automatically. This behavior is controlled by the `auto-insert` variable, which determines whether to insert something when a new empty file is visited. [1]

results.answer: Yes, you can have the matching bracket highlighted when your cursor is next to one using the option `show-paren-highlight-openparen`. This option, when set to a non-`nil` value (i.e., enabled), highlights an open paren when point is just before it. Since this behavior applies to all delimiters including brackets, it will work for matching brackets when the cursor is next to them [1] (and also referenced in [2] for periphery cases). I keep retyping the same long macro after restarting, can I save it in my config
results.answer: Yes, you can save a keyboard macro in your config file so it persists across Emacs sessions. In Viper, you can use the command `(viper-record-kbd-macro)` to save a macro in your Viper customization file, which will make it permanently available [2] . For example, to save a macro named "gg" for use in the Insert state in buffer 'my-buf', you would use the command: `(viper-record-kbd-macro "gg" 'insert-state [1] up (meta x) next-line return "my-buf")` [2] . This way, the macro will be available in future Emacs sessions when you start Viper. If you're using Emacs directly, you can save the macro definition using `M-x insert-kbd-macro` and then save the file, which can be loaded later with `load-file` [1]

results.question: use-package lazy load bind key
results.answer: The correct way to achieve lazy loading of key bindings in `use-package` is by using the `:defer t` keyword to delay loading the package until needed, combined with `:bind` to define key bindings. However, the key binding itself is not lazy-loaded by default — it is applied when the package is loaded, and if the package is deferred, the binding will be applied after the package is loaded (i.e., when the user first uses it). This is achieved via `:defer t` and `:bind`, as described in extract [4] and [5] — the binding is set up during package loading, which is deferred by `:defer t`. Thus, the lazy load of key bindings is enabled by using `:defer t` with `:bind`. The binding is not applied until the package is actually loaded, which happens lazily when the user triggers the command or key sequence. This is consistent with the manual's explanation that `:defer t` postpones loading until needed [4] and that bindings are applied after the package loads [5]

results.question: how do I edit a remtoe file on another server through scp without copying it first
results.answer: Use the `ssh` method in TRAMP to edit a remote file directly, without copying it first. For example, edit `/etc/motd` on `otherhost` with: `C-x C-f /ssh:root@otherhost:/etc/motd <RET>`. This uses SSH for secure access and editing, bypassing file copying [1] and [2] (note: TRAMP's direct editing via SSH does not require copying the file first). The `scp` method is for file transfer, not editing [3] — editing is done via SSH session. Thus, the correct method is `ssh` in TRAMP. [1]

results.question: how do I pop up a clickable outline of sections for my latex paper, I keep forgeting where things are

Note that the TOC buffer shows only sections by default, but you can use ‘l’ and ‘i’ to display labels and index entries as well [4] . results.question: how do I sotre a link to the place I'm at in my notes
results.answer: Use `M-x org-store-link` to store a link to the current location in your Org file [1] . This command stores a link that can be inserted later into an Org buffer, and it will point to the current headline or named block if available. If you're in a notes file, this will store a link to your current position. For Org mode buffers, if there's a named block or headline at point, it will link to that; otherwise, it links to the current headline. This is the standard way to store a link to your current position in an Org file, including notes. [1]
